full_judgment: 14. The nature of legal relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1, if any, is yet another crucial question. The plaintiff consistently and persistently asserted that the defendant No. 1 is a representative and agent of overseas buyers of garments and suppliers of fabrics. If that be correct then the plaintiffs claim that the defendant No. 1 is not entitled to any technical fee because he failed to render technical services, loses all its legal significance for the reason that if he acted for his principal, then the question as to the said party's entitlement to the technical fee is definitely a matter between him and his principal. In his petition, the plaintiff claimed that he suffered loss because of defendant No.1’s breaches and that is why he said defendant cannot get any technical fee. In. this respect one has to keep in mind, as has been stated by Cheshire and Fiffot in their- book "Law of Contract", 13th edition, page 483, "the general rule is not only that the principal acquires rights and liabilities, but also that the agent drops out and ceases to be a party to the contract," if he acts qua agent. The principal is bound, as regards third parties, by all the acts of the agent under the maxim "Qui facit per alium, facit per se. " Anson's Law of Contract, Twenty-fifth edition, page 626, states, "since an agent is employed to establish privity of contract between his principal and a third party, it is the general rule that he acquires no rights and incurs no liability." He can of course be used by his principal under "agent-principal" contractual relationship (White vs Lincoln 1803, 8 Yes. Jun 363). But he is not himself a party to any contract entered into by his principal through him with a third party if he posed as a disclosed agent of his principal and, as such, no question of his liability to such a third party for any breach can arise. There are, however a few circumstances of exception where an agent can be liable. These exceptions include a situation (1) when an agent is a party to a deed, not as a constituted attorney, but as a party, (2) if he signs negotiable instrument without authority, (3) if principal is non-existent, (4) if the agent is guilty of misrepresentation, (5) if he does not disclose existence of any principal and projects himself as the principal, (6) if he acts without authority, (7) if he expressly or impliedly assumes personal liability, (8) if trade usage or customs make him liable, (9) if he actually contracts on his own behalf,(10) if he refuses to identify the principal. It is always a question of construction by which the presumed intention of the parties is to be assessed, as far as available from the circumstances. Such an intention, if clearly evident, is decisive, but if not, the general principle shall apply which dictates that the contract is the contract of the principal, not that of the agent, and prima facie in law the only person who can be sued is the principal (Montgomerie vs United Kingdom Mutual SS Association 1891, I QB 370). In Pacquin vs Beanclerk (1906 AC 148) also it was observed that an agent possesses neither rights nor liabilities. This is more so if the agency is a disclosed one. A disclosed agency therefore, creates a refutable presumption that it is the principal, and not the agent, who is the contracting party. The prima facie rule that if the contract is made for a named principal then the principal alone can sue or be sued, is however a refutable presumption of purely general character. At one time, it used to be perceived that a person who contracted for a foreign principal should be regarded as having contracted as a principal to the exclusion of foreign principal (Elbinger AG Fur Fabrication Von Fisonbahn Material vs Clay-1873 LR, 8 QB 313). But with the vast increase in international trade, this particular usage has steadily waned and has now disappeared (Teheran-Euro Ltd vs ST Belton (Tractor) Ltd 1986, 2 All ER 886). No doubt the plaintiff will have ample opportunity to try to resolve the dichotomy arising from terming the defendant No.1 as an agent on the one hand and trying to impose contractual. liability on him on the other hand, at the time of the trial by adducing evidence and advancing intrinsic legal submission and, perhaps by showing that the defendant No. 1 falls within one of the exceptions, but as far as we are concerned, and insofar as it is an appeal against the rejection of temporary injunction application, only with limited affidavit evidence before us, we found nothing to enable us to deviate from the general principle and we take such a state of affairs as the plaintiffs failure to make out a prime facie case.
